chapters.title: Two Kitchens, One Recipe
chapters.scope: Start from zero: a program is a list of instructions the computer follows in order; source code (the text you write) vs the running program; JavaScript the language (its official name is ECMAScript) vs the host it runs in: the same recipe language is cooked in different kitchens, the browser kitchen (a page counter, the DOM) and the Node kitchen (a pantry of files), plus Deno and Bun; the engine (V8 in Chrome and Node, SpiderMonkey in Firefox, JavaScriptCore in Safari) is the cook who reads the recipe; language features vs host APIs (`console`, `document`, `fs` come from the kitchen, not the language; believing `console.log` is part of the language is a common wrong idea); editions are named by year (ES2015 = ES6; ES2026 is the 17th edition, the current standard); JavaScript is not Java; interpreted plus JIT at a cartoon level; why one language runs in browsers, servers and tools. Then set up and run: install Node (LTS vs Current; this book is pinned to Node 26 LTS), check with `node --version` (and `npm --version`), terminal basics (`cd`, `ls`, paths, which folder you are in), create `hello.js` in an editor (VS Code), save before you run, run it with `node hello.js`; the first program is one `console.log("Hello, world!")` line (just "the print instruction" here); the REPL (`node`, the `Welcome to Node.js v26.13.0.` banner, `.help`, `.exit`), the REPL echoes each result, and after `let a = 1` it echoes `undefined`, which is not an error; REPL echo vs `console.log`; when to use the REPL vs a file (a 20-line program belongs in a file); the browser DevTools console as a second REPL; `node --watch hello.js` re-runs on save; file extensions. Read the first real errors like a detective (name, message, file and line): running browser code in Node gives `ReferenceError: alert is not defined`, `ReferenceError: document is not defined`, `ReferenceError: prompt is not defined` (the Node kitchen has no page); running from the wrong folder gives `Error: Cannot find module '/path/app.js'` with code `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`; classic slips: typing shell commands into the REPL, forgetting to save, reading the REPL's `undefined` as a failure.

chapters.title: Sentences and Jars
chapters.scope: Syntax and output: a program is made of statements (sentences that do something) and expressions (pieces that produce a value); the semicolon as a full stop, and automatic semicolon insertion (ASI) as a gremlin that sometimes writes it in for you and sometimes in the wrong place (`return` alone on a line returns `undefined`, with no error); whitespace and indentation do not change meaning; JavaScript is case-sensitive (`Console.log` gives `ReferenceError: Console is not defined`); comments `//` and `/* */`; `console.log` with several arguments separated by spaces; string vs number output (`console.log(1, "1", 1 + 1, "1" + 1)` prints `1 1 2 11`); `"use strict"` and the fact that modules and classes are strict automatically; reserved words; the anatomy of a first error (file:line, the source line, the caret `^`, `Name: message`), and that a SyntaxError means the file could not be parsed so no line ran: missing bracket `SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{'` (from `if (x > 0 {`), unclosed block `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of input`, unterminated string `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token`. Values and types: seven primitives (number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol; bigint and symbol only named) and objects as the one non-primitive; literals; `typeof` and every result it gives; `typeof function` is `"function"`; `typeof null === "object"` is a historic bug from 1995 (so a null check via typeof fails); `typeof []` is `"object"` and `Array.isArray` is the real check; undefined ("never set") vs null ("empty on purpose"); `NaN` has type number; `"5"` and `5` are different things.

chapters.title: Tags and the Number Line
chapters.scope: Variables: declaration vs assignment vs initialization; `let` and `const` (`const` must be initialized and cannot be reassigned); a variable is a name tag tied to a value, not a box: `const` glues the tag to one value, `let` lets you move it; naming rules (letters, `$`, `_`, digits not first), camelCase, reserved words, meaningful names; `const` by default; reassignment; swapping two variables with a temporary; dynamic typing (one variable can hold any type over time); `const` objects can still be changed inside (preview only). Mistakes with real errors: reassigning a const `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.`; declaring twice `SyntaxError: Identifier 'd' has already been declared`; a name starting with a digit `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token`; using an undeclared name `ReferenceError: x is not defined`; `if (x = 5)` assigns instead of compares, with no error (shown here, revisited in ch6). Numbers: integers and decimals are one `number` type; `+ - * / % **`; precedence and parentheses (`2 ** 3 ** 2` groups to the right); unary minus; `%` takes the sign of the left operand (`-5 % 3` is `-2`, `-7 % 3`); `++`/`--` prefix vs postfix inside expressions (`let a = 5; let b = a++ + ++a;`); compound assignment `+=`; `1/0` is `Infinity` (not an error), `-Infinity`, `NaN`; `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004` and `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false` (floats are a ruler with marks only at binary fractions); `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`; `Math.round`/`floor`/`ceil`/`trunc`/`max`/`min`/`abs`/`random`; `Math.floor(-3.5)` is `-4` but `Math.trunc(-3.5)` is `-3`; integer division with `Math.floor`/`Math.trunc`; picking a rounding function ("pages needed" needs `Math.ceil`); `toFixed` returns a string, `(1.005).toFixed(2)` is `"1.00"`, and `(1.5).toFixed(101)` gives `RangeError: toFixed() digits argument must be between 0 and 100`.

chapters.title: Doorkeepers and Translators
chapters.scope: Booleans and strict equality: `true`/`false`; `> < >= <=`; `===` and `!==` as the default; truthy vs falsy, with the doorkeeper's list of exactly 8 falsy values (`false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`) and everyone else gets in; `Boolean()` and `!!`; surprises `Boolean("false")`, `Boolean("0")` and `!![]` are all `true`; `NaN !== NaN`, so `x === NaN` is always false; `Number.isNaN`; `Object.is` (mention); objects and arrays compare by identity (`[] === []` and `[1,2,3] === [1,2,3]` are `false`); `"1" === 1` is false. Type conversion and coercion: explicit `Number()`, `String()`, `Boolean()`, `parseInt`/`parseFloat` (radix; stop at the first non-digit), unary `+`; `Number("")` is 0, `Number(" 12 ")` is 12, `Number("08px")` is NaN while `parseInt("08px")` is 8, `Number(null)` is 0 but `Number(undefined)` is NaN; implicit: `+` with a string concatenates (`"5" + 3` is `"53"`) while `- * /` convert to number (`"5" - 3` is 2); text that should be a number (`let count = "5"; count += 1` gives `"51"`; a total that prints "1020" instead of 30); `==` conversion rules as the translator robot's rulebook: `null == undefined` is true, `null == 0` is false but `null >= 0` is true, `0 == ""` and `0 == "0"` are true but `"" == "0"` is false (not transitive); `[] + []` is `""`, `[] + {}` is `"[object Object]"`; the 'wat' quiz: `'b' + 'a' + +'a' + 'a'` is `"baNaNa"`, `['1','2','3'].map(parseInt)` is `[1, NaN, NaN]` (shown, explained in ch9); type errors that refuse to coerce: `1n + 1` gives `TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions`, `Symbol() + ''` gives `TypeError: Cannot convert a Symbol value to a string`; choosing `Number` vs `parseInt` for "12px"; why to prefer `===`.

chapters.title: Vending Machines and Recipe Cards
chapters.scope: Functions I: why functions (naming and reuse); declaration syntax; calling with `()`; parameters vs arguments; `return` ends the function and hands back a value; no return gives `undefined`; missing arguments are `undefined`, extra arguments are ignored; default parameters; local variables; print vs return (a vending machine: parameters are coin slots, `return` drops the snack in the tray, `console.log` only shouts its name), so the caller of a print-only function gets `undefined`; pure vs side-effecting; functions calling functions; verbs as function names; forgetting `()` passes the function itself (`console.log(greet)` prints `[Function: greet]`); `greet()` with no argument then `name.toUpperCase()` gives `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase')`; calling a non-function gives `TypeError: f is not a function`. Functions II: function expressions and anonymous functions; arrow functions (concise body returns implicitly, a braced body needs `return`, returning an object needs `({ })`, so `() => { id: 1 }` returns `undefined`); functions as values stored in variables, arrays and objects; passing a function as an argument (a callback: a recipe card handed to a helper); passing vs calling (`setTimeout(greet(), 1000)` calls immediately); returning a function (preview of closures); `arguments` vs rest `...args` (mention); declarations are hoisted but expressions are not: calling a `var` function expression early gives `TypeError: notYet is not a function`, a `let`/`const` one gives `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'f' before initialization`.

chapters.scope: Arrays I: array literal, a crate of numbered boxes from 0 (train = string, ch2); `.length`; reading out of range gives `undefined` (`arr[arr.length]`); writing to an index; `push`/`pop` at the back and `shift`/`unshift` at the slow front (everyone renumbers); their return values (`arr.push(4)` returns the new length, not the array); `includes`, `indexOf`, `at(-1)`; `slice` copies vs `splice` mutates (and the mixup bug); `concat`; nested arrays as a grid; holes (`[1,,3]` prints `[ 1, <1 empty item>, 3 ]`); `length = 0` empties an array; `Array.isArray` and `typeof []` is `"object"`; `const arr = []` still allows `arr.push` (const is not frozen); `new Array(-1)` gives `RangeError: Invalid array length`. chapters.scope: Performance and memory basics, a kitchen at rush hour: Big-O intuition (O(1), O(n), O(n²)) for 6 snippets; Map/Set lookup vs `array.includes` inside a loop (nested includes on 100k items; replace a nested loop with a Set); measuring with `performance.now()` and `console.time`, and why benchmarks are non-deterministic (timings change every run); premature micro-optimizations; DevTools Performance and Memory panels; `node --cpu-prof` (mention); reachability and garbage collection; common leaks (forgotten listeners, timers, closures, growing caches; `WeakMap` as the fix); debounce and throttle; not blocking the event loop (chunking work; Web Workers and `worker_threads` as a preview); lazy loading with dynamic `import()`.
